Corn_(maize)___Cercospora_leaf_spot Gray.description: Fungal leaf infection affecting maize caused by Cercospora zeae-maydis, flourishing in warm, humid climates with prolonged leaf wetness.
Corn_(maize)___Cercospora_leaf_spot Gray.symptoms: Narrow, rectangular, tan-to-gray lesions running parallel to leaf veins with sharp boundaries, coalescing to cause premature blight.
Corn_(maize)___Cercospora_leaf_spot Gray.cultural_practices: Rotate crops with non-host species (such as soybean or legumes) for at least one year; till crop debris into soil where erosion permits; ensure adequate plant spacing for airflow.
Corn_(maize)___Cercospora_leaf_spot Gray.biological_control: Use resistant or tolerant maize hybrid cultivars certified by national or state agricultural universities.
Corn_(maize)___Cercospora_leaf_spot Gray.chemical_reference: Chemical fungicides should strictly follow state agricultural extension guidelines. Consult your local Krishi Vigyan Kendra (KVK) or extension officer for approved schedules and safety intervals.
Corn_(maize)___Cercospora_leaf_spot Gray.source_title: ICAR - Indian Institute of Maize Research Disease Management Guide

Corn_(maize)___Common_rust_.description: Fungal disease caused by Puccinia sorghi occurring prominently under moderate temperatures (16-25°C) and high relative humidity.
Corn_(maize)___Common_rust_.symptoms: Small, powdery, cinnamon-brown to reddish pustules scattered over both upper and lower leaf surfaces, becoming brownish-black as plants mature.
Corn_(maize)___Common_rust_.cultural_practices: Plant early in the season to evade peak airborne spore deposition; ensure balanced potassium and nitrogen soil nutrition; remove volunteer corn hosts.
Corn_(maize)___Common_rust_.biological_control: Deploy resistant hybrids possessing specific Rp resistance genes approved in your agro-climatic zone.
Corn_(maize)___Common_rust_.chemical_reference: Consult your local agricultural extension service for recommended, locally registered fungicides and post-harvest intervals.
Corn_(maize)___Common_rust_.source_title: State Agricultural University Maize Pathology Extension Bulletin

Corn_(maize)___Northern_Leaf_Blight.description: Destructive fungal disease caused by Exserohilum turcicum, capable of causing heavy grain yield losses if infection strikes prior to silking.
Corn_(maize)___Northern_Leaf_Blight.symptoms: Long, elliptical, grayish-green or tan cigar-shaped lesions (2.5 to 15 cm long) with smooth margins, developing dark fungal spore zones in damp weather.
Corn_(maize)___Northern_Leaf_Blight.cultural_practices: Practice minimum two-year crop rotation; bury infected crop residue post-harvest; avoid dense planting densities.
Corn_(maize)___Northern_Leaf_Blight.biological_control: Sow certified resistant cultivars with Ht polygenic resistance traits.
Corn_(maize)___Northern_Leaf_Blight.chemical_reference: Refer to certified university extension guides or the nearest Krishi Vigyan Kendra for approved regional fungicides.
Corn_(maize)___Northern_Leaf_Blight.source_title: ICAR-IIMR Northern Corn Leaf Blight Advisory

Corn_(maize)___healthy.description: Normal, vigorous maize foliage free of active pathogenic lesions, chlorosis, or necrotic spotting.
Corn_(maize)___healthy.symptoms: Even green coloration, intact leaf margins, strong midrib structure, and normal venation.
Corn_(maize)___healthy.cultural_practices: Maintain regular scouting schedules, balanced N-P-K fertilization, and uniform drip or furrow irrigation.
Corn_(maize)___healthy.biological_control: Continue integrated pest management (IPM) to preserve beneficial predatory insects.
Corn_(maize)___healthy.chemical_reference: No chemical intervention warranted. Continue monitoring.
Corn_(maize)___healthy.source_title: ICAR Good Agricultural Practices for Maize

Potato___Early_blight.description: Prevalent foliar fungal disease caused by Alternaria solani, often striking stressed, mature, or nutrient-deficient potato foliage.
Potato___Early_blight.symptoms: Dark brown to black necrotic spots with characteristic concentric rings creating a target-board pattern, typically starting on older lower foliage.
Potato___Early_blight.cultural_practices: Ensure optimal plant vigor via balanced nitrogen; avoid sprinkler irrigation that wets foliage late in the day; practice 3-year crop rotation avoiding solanaceous crops.
Potato___Early_blight.biological_control: Plant certified disease-free seed tubers of tolerant varieties.
Potato___Early_blight.chemical_reference: Follow protective fungicide guidance strictly per State Agricultural Extension schedules. Consult your local agricultural officer for certified options.
Potato___Early_blight.source_title: ICAR - Central Potato Research Institute (CPRI) Disease Guide
Potato___Early_blight.reviewer_name: Dr. A. K. Sen, Senior Plant Pathologist

Potato___Late_blight.description: High-impact disease caused by the oomycete Phytophthora infestans, capable of rapidly devastating potato foliage and tubers in cool, humid conditions.
Potato___Late_blight.symptoms: Irregular water-soaked brown lesions with pale green or chlorotic borders on leaves, displaying white fungal-like downy growth on undersides during high humidity.
Potato___Late_blight.cultural_practices: Destroy cull piles and volunteer potatoes; hill soil well around rows to protect tubers; remove diseased foliage prior to tuber harvest.
Potato___Late_blight.biological_control: Utilize certified resistant potato cultivars recommended by CPRI for your region.
Potato___Late_blight.chemical_reference: Apply protective treatments only in consultation with your local agricultural extension service. Strict adherence to approved products is required.
Potato___Late_blight.reviewer_name: Dr. A. K. Sen, Senior Plant Pathologist

Potato___healthy.description: Vigorous, unblemished potato foliage demonstrating normal chlorophyll density and structure.
Potato___healthy.symptoms: Uniform deep green color, absence of lesions or water-soaked halos, smooth leaflet margins.
Potato___healthy.cultural_practices: Maintain regular field scouting, balanced hilling, and monitored irrigation without prolonged foliage wetting.
Potato___healthy.biological_control: Preserve natural beneficial predators and practice crop hygiene.
Potato___healthy.chemical_reference: No treatment required. Continue regular scouting.
Potato___healthy.reviewer_name: Dr. A. K. Sen, Senior Plant Pathologist

Tomato___Bacterial_spot.description: Bacterial disease caused by Xanthomonas species, thriving in warm, rainy weather with overhead splashing.
Tomato___Bacterial_spot.symptoms: Small, dark, water-soaked circular or angular spots on leaves, becoming brown and necrotic with yellow haloes, leading to defoliation.
Tomato___Bacterial_spot.cultural_practices: Avoid overhead watering; disinfect tools and stakes; rotate away from solanaceous crops for minimum 2 years; do not work in wet fields.
Tomato___Bacterial_spot.biological_control: Use certified pathogen-free seeds and disease-resistant seedling transplants.
Tomato___Bacterial_spot.chemical_reference: Copper-based bactericides and certified treatments must strictly comply with regional Krishi Vigyan Kendra advisories.
Tomato___Bacterial_spot.source_title: Indian Institute of Vegetable Research (IIVR) Tomato Advisory

Tomato___Early_blight.description: Fungal disease caused by Alternaria linariae/solani, affecting tomato leaves, stems, and fruits.
Tomato___Early_blight.symptoms: Brown to black circular spots with concentric target-board rings, starting on lower leaves and yellowing surrounding tissue.
Tomato___Early_blight.cultural_practices: Stake and prune lower leaves to improve air circulation; apply organic mulch to prevent soil splashing; rotate with non-solanaceous crops.
Tomato___Early_blight.biological_control: Select resistant varieties and use certified disease-free nursery stock.
Tomato___Early_blight.chemical_reference: Refer to local agricultural extension officers for approved fungicide applications and pre-harvest intervals.

Tomato___Late_blight.description: Fast-moving oomycete infection (Phytophthora infestans) that can defoliate entire tomato fields within days during cool, rainy weather.
Tomato___Late_blight.symptoms: Large, irregular water-soaked pale-to-dark gray lesions with oily margins; white mildew-like sporulation on the underside of leaves under humid conditions.
Tomato___Late_blight.cultural_practices: Space plants widely; avoid wetting foliage; promptly remove and destroy all infected plant residues; do not compost blighted material.
Tomato___Late_blight.biological_control: Plant resistant cultivars with Ph-2 and Ph-3 resistance genes where locally available.
Tomato___Late_blight.chemical_reference: Promptly consult your regional agricultural extension agent for emergency treatment protocols approved by state authorities.

Tomato___Leaf_Mold.description: Fungal disease caused by Passalora fulva, most prevalent in polyhouses and humid enclosed conditions with high relative humidity (>85%).
Tomato___Leaf_Mold.symptoms: Pale greenish-yellow chlorotic spots on upper leaf surfaces matching olive-green to brown velvety fungal patches on lower surfaces.
Tomato___Leaf_Mold.cultural_practices: Enhance ventilation and airflow through polyhouses/shade-nets; space plants adequately; drip irrigate to keep foliage dry.
Tomato___Leaf_Mold.biological_control: Choose tomato cultivars carrying Cf resistance genes.
Tomato___Leaf_Mold.chemical_reference: Follow state agricultural university schedules for protected cultivation fungicides. Consult your extension agent.

Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.description: Foliar fungal pathogen caused by Septoria lycopersici, thriving in warm, damp environments with prolonged leaf moisture.
Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.symptoms: Numerous small circular spots (1-3 mm) with dark brown margins and sunken grayish-white centers dotted with tiny black fruiting bodies (pycnidia).
Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.cultural_practices: Mulch soil around plants; remove infected lower leaves; avoid overhead irrigation; clean stakes and cages thoroughly between seasons.
Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.biological_control: Ensure use of certified clean seeds and sanitized nursery media.
Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.chemical_reference: Consult your local Krishi Vigyan Kendra for recommended fungicide sprays and protective rotations.

Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.description: Arachnid pest (Tetranychus urticae) attacking leaves by puncturing plant cells, prevalent in hot, dry, dusty weather.
Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.symptoms: Fine yellow-white stippling on leaf upper surfaces, bronze or yellow leaf drying, and delicate fine webbing on leaf undersides and growing tips.
Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.cultural_practices: Maintain adequate irrigation to reduce plant water stress; wash foliage with clean water mist in dry heat; suppress dust on field borders.
Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.biological_control: Release or conserve predatory phytoseiid mites (e.g. Phytoseiulus persimilis) and avoid broad-spectrum insecticides that kill natural predators.
Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.chemical_reference: Acaricides must be strictly used according to certified agricultural university guidance. Consult your local extension officer.
Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.source_title: ICAR Integrated Pest Management for Horticultural Crops

Tomato___Target_Spot.description: Fungal infection caused by Corynespora cassiicola, flourishing in warm, humid regions with frequent rainfall.
Tomato___Target_Spot.symptoms: Small brown necrotic lesions that enlarge with concentric target rings, frequently surrounded by a yellow chlorotic halo.
Tomato___Target_Spot.cultural_practices: Improve air drainage by pruning suckers; discard fallen diseased leaves; rotate away from solanaceous and cucurbit crops.
Tomato___Target_Spot.biological_control: Plant tolerant hybrids and use pathogen-free nursery transplants.
Tomato___Target_Spot.chemical_reference: Consult certified agricultural extension agents for regional registered fungicide recommendations.

Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.description: Geminivirus (TYLCV) transmitted by the sweetpotato whitefly (Bemisia tabaci), causing severe stunting and leaf deformation.
Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.symptoms: Upward curling and cupping of leaflets, marked chlorosis/yellowing of leaf margins, reduced leaf size, stunting, and bushy upright growth.
Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.cultural_practices: Install 40-50 mesh insect-proof netting in nurseries; erect yellow sticky traps for whitefly monitoring; rogue and destroy infected plants promptly.
Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.biological_control: Cultivate TYLCV-resistant hybrids carrying Ty-1, Ty-2, or Ty-3 resistance genes.
Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.chemical_reference: Direct viral cure does not exist. Whitefly vector management must adhere strictly to ICAR extension recommendations.

Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.description: Tobamovirus (ToMV) that is mechanically transmitted with high persistence on seeds, tools, hands, and plant debris.
Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.symptoms: Light and dark green mosaic mottle on leaves, distorted or fern-like leaf growth, stunting, and brown internal fruit necrosis.
Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.cultural_practices: Wash hands and disinfect pruning tools with 10% trisodium phosphate (TSP) or skimmed milk; prohibit smoking or handling raw tobacco near crops; remove infected plants.
Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.biological_control: Use certified ToMV-resistant tomato seeds and varieties with Tm-2 resistance genes.
Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.chemical_reference: No chemical viricide exists. Sanitation and vector prevention are critical. Consult your local extension service.

Tomato___healthy.description: Vibrant, healthy tomato foliage with balanced vegetative vigor and no visible disease symptoms.
Tomato___healthy.symptoms: Uniform deep green foliage, robust leaflet margins, absence of spots, lesions, chlorosis, or wilting.
Tomato___healthy.cultural_practices: Continue scheduled crop scouting, balanced fertigation, soil moisture maintenance, and regular trellising.
Tomato___healthy.biological_control: Maintain ecological balance by fostering natural predatory insects.
Tomato___healthy.chemical_reference: No intervention required. Continue regular scouting.
Tomato___healthy.source_title: ICAR Good Agricultural Practices for Tomato
